overview: The atlas id huns represents a North Caucasian polity centered on Varachan in present-day Dagestan, not Attila's fifth-century empire. Armenian accounts call it the Country or Kingdom of the Huns; whether its people should be equated with Sabirs or Suvars remains debated. In 661-682 its forces raided Caucasian Albania, negotiated peace, and operated under Alp Ilutuer, a ruler tied by title and marriage to the Khazar qaghan. Bishop Israel's winter mission reached Varachan in 682. Its Christian narrative describes a city, royal camps, nobles, commoners, craftspeople, sacred trees, horse sacrifice, funerary contests, assemblies, and diplomatic letters, but conversion probably remained limited. Arab-Khazar wars transformed the region: armies struck settlements north of Derbent in 723, and Marwan's 737 campaign captured or destroyed Varachan in later reconstructions. The atlas paints one tidy polygon only from 700 to 800. It includes much of Dagestan and Chechnya, meets Khazar, Alan, Sabir, and Caucasian Albanian layers, then becomes Khazar space. The card uses circa 660-737, marks the ending as transformation, and keeps these Huns separate from both the Hunnic Empire and neighboring Sabirs.

periods.title: 660 to 670: northern raiders appear as Huns
periods.summary: Armenian sources distinguish raiders called Huns from the Khazars in attacks on Caucasian Albania around 661-662. Their political formation and precise territory remain uncertain. The card begins circa 660 because this is the first secure cluster of records for the exact later North Caucasian polity, not a documented founding ceremony.

periods.title: 670 to 681: Khazar power grows and Alp Ilutuer negotiates
periods.summary: As Khazar authority emerged north of the Caucasus, Alp Ilutuer led a Hunnic force into Albania, taking people, livestock, and goods. An Albanian church envoy negotiated peace. The Turkic title ilteber and a reported marriage to the qaghan's daughter suggest subordinate alliance, although the polity retained its own ruler and diplomacy.

periods.title: 681 to 682: Israel crosses the Caucasus to Varachan
periods.summary: Bishop Israel left on 23 December 681 with gifts, supplies, and companions. After a winter journey through Albania, mountain routes, and the Derbent gate, he reached Varachan around Lent in 682. The detailed itinerary anchors the polity geographically more securely than any modern attempt to draw its full frontier.

periods.title: 682 to 690: elite conversion, resistance, and embassies
periods.summary: The Christian narrative says Alp Ilutuer, grandees, soldiers, and townspeople heard Israel, while ritual specialists resisted destruction of sacred sites. The ruler requested Israel as a permanent bishop and sent envoys and letters south. Scholarship treats the episode as elite diplomacy and sporadic conversion, not proof that every household became Christian.

periods.title: 690 to 705: the polity persists within Khazar ascendancy
periods.summary: Evidence becomes thin after Israel's mission. North Caucasian Huns remained connected to the expanding Khazar realm, while local communities, camps, and settlements did not lose every identity at once. The period is therefore described as political subordination and continuity, not as an invented sequence of named rulers or a homogeneous population.

periods.title: 705 to 723: Arab-Khazar war presses the Caspian corridor
periods.summary: Arab and Khazar forces repeatedly contested Derbent and routes north of the Caucasus. Armies, garrisons, raiders, captives, and provisioning demands affected smaller polities between them. In 723 al-Jarrah advanced through the region and later reconstructions associate Vabandar or Varachan with the campaign, though names and locations are disputed.

periods.title: 723 to 730: settlements face repeated campaigns
periods.summary: After the 723 invasion, warfare continued around Balanjar, Derbent, and the Caspian foothills. Reports of huge house counts or army sizes are literary numbers, not censuses. They still show that writers imagined substantial settled centers alongside mobile camps, and that the frontier required food, animals, labor, fortifications, and negotiation.

periods.title: 730 to 737: Marwan's campaign transforms Varachan
periods.summary: Khazar armies reached deep into the caliphate in 730, followed by escalating counter-campaigns. In 737 Marwan invaded through the Caucasus; later Armenian and Arabic traditions connect the offensive with Varachan or Khamzin and describe capture and destruction. The endpoint marks political transformation, not the disappearance of residents or every Hunnic name.

sections.title: Identify these Huns, their neighbors, and map

items.text: The repository indexes exact id huns simply as “Huns,” dated approximately 700 to 800 from historical basemaps. Coverage records one border file and a missing review. No card or override explains that this eastern Caucasus feature is different from the already researched fifth-century Hunnic Empire.

All fifty border snapshots were decoded. Exact id huns appears only in world-700, with properties 700 to 800 and precision one. It is one valid Polygon, one ring, and twenty-eight positions, absent from 600, 800, 900, and 1000. The perfect century is an atlas convention, not a dated foundation.

The polygon spans roughly 45.031 to 48.253 east and 42.057 to 44.189 north. Varachan-Qaytaq, Chir-Yurt, Balanjar, Semender, Tarki, Sulak, and thirteen other probes fall inside; Derbent, Vladikavkaz, Astrakhan, Tbilisi, Baku, and Yerevan stay outside. This is reconstructed coverage, not surveyed sovereignty.

Direct arc seams meet Khazars, Alans, Sabirs, and Caucasian Albania once each, without positive-area overlap. At 800 nearly every tested core point becomes Khazar while Baku becomes Abbasid, and huns never returns. That supports broad regional relabeling, not a single dated conquest; written evidence instead supports circa 660 to 737.

“Hun” was a broad external label. Some scholars equate Varachan's polity with Savirs or Suvars; others see a local union, and the atlas draws huns and sabirs separately. Its contact zone was multilingual, so the card neither merges exact records nor assigns one language to every person. Crisp map colors had no interpreter.

sections.title: Govern through courts, camps, assemblies, and diplomacy

items.text: Movses describes Alp Ilutuer consulting grandees and lords, receiving a bishop at a royal court, and issuing orders across multiple royal camps. This reveals a mobile and settled political world together. It does not establish a centralized bureaucracy with modern departments, uniform taxes, or permanent officials in every district.

In 681 the Hunnic force included armored cavalry, archers, banners, commanders, and allied contingents. It raided villages, took livestock, goods, and captives, then withdrew after negotiation. The account is hostile to the attackers, but it makes the human cost of frontier warfare clearer than a moving border line.

Caucasian Albania sent senior clergy as peace envoys because annual Hunnic attacks and Arab taxation strained the country from opposite directions. Gifts, travel provisions, letters, interpreters, and ritual courtesy supported diplomacy. Peace was produced through labor and communication, not simply announced by two rulers meeting on a timeline.

The mission narrative stages a crowded public tribunal where ritual specialists, bishop, ruler, nobles, soldiers, and citizens disputed belief. Because a Christian author shaped the scene, its unanimity and speeches require caution. It nevertheless shows that public persuasion, coercion, and assembly were imaginable instruments of Hunnic government.

Alp Ilutuer sent two named chiefs south with letters requesting Israel's return. These envoys linked Varachan to Albanian and Armenian authorities and made religion part of alliance building. The preserved letters are Armenian literary documents; they demonstrate diplomatic memory more securely than verbatim Hunnic composition.

sections.title: Move, settle, herd, trade, and make things

items.text: Sources place a city at Varachan while also mentioning many royal camps and describing much of the population as mobile. Households likely combined pastoral movement with settlements and markets in different proportions. “Nomad” should not erase craftspeople, stored food, cultivated plots, political buildings, or residents who moved only seasonally.

The Caspian coastal corridor narrowed at Derbent between mountains and sea. Its Sasanian walls, gates, harbor, and mountain barrier shaped travel long before and after this polity. Hunnic raiders and envoys used the route, but the reviewed sources do not prove that Varachan permanently administered the fortress.

Horses supported cavalry, status, racing, diplomacy, and sacrifice; captured herds also mattered as wealth and food security. Cattle and other livestock moved during raids. These references illuminate elite and military priorities better than exact herd composition, ownership rules, women's work, or the seasonal schedule of ordinary pastoral families.

At Varachan, Israel reportedly summoned skilled woodworkers to turn a felled sacred tree into a decorated cross with carved, painted, silver, and nailed elements. The episode is polemical, yet it securely implies specialists, tools, materials, and coordinated labor. Theology arrived with a surprisingly detailed carpentry order.

Chir-Yurt burials show varied orientations and biological diversity in the Sulak lowlands; pottery links also cross regional traditions. Archaeologists cautiously propose a Savir component rather than assigning every grave to one people. Objects can reveal contact and practice, but they do not carry identity cards into the excavation trench.

sections.title: Eat, host, and organize household life

items.text: The mission traveled with prepared rations and received lodging, honors, and prolonged hospitality in cities along the route and at Varachan. Such scenes show that feeding guests and retinues carried political meaning. They do not provide menus, calorie counts, or evidence that ordinary households could sustain courtly generosity.

A later regional collection associates Hunnic hospitality scenes with horse or camel milk and flatbread cooked on a metal griddle. These details are plausible for pastoral households but rest on mediated texts. The card presents them as reported foods, not a universal daily breakfast served across the entire polygon.

Sacrificial animals were eaten and their blood, heads, or skins dedicated at sacred trees according to the Christian account. That evidence connects food, livestock, worship, and communal gathering, while the author's disgust distorts the view. A ritual meal cannot stand in for every supper prepared in Varachan.

Movses condemns levirate or plural-marriage practices and claims brothers could share a wife. These statements come from a reforming cleric cataloguing pagan error, so prevalence is unknowable. They still show that marriage, inheritance, and household continuity were contested arenas, especially when missionaries challenged existing kin arrangements.

At the ruling level, marriage connected Alp Ilutuer to the Khazar qaghan's family; below that level, evidence for spouses, parents, children, residence, and inheritance is scarce. Captivity could violently break households during raids. The card keeps ordinary families visible by naming this documentary silence rather than inventing a model household.

sections.title: Practice religion, mourning, sport, and public ceremony

items.text: The Armenian account describes reverence for a sky power, sacred trees, lightning-struck beings or objects, roads, moon, fire, and water. Iranica cautions that Iranian names may reflect the writer's translation of unfamiliar beliefs. The evidence supports a layered ritual world, not a tidy standardized creed called “Tengrism.”

Funerals reportedly included lament, drums, whistling, self-cutting, sword contests, wrestling, horse racing, and dancing. The Christian narrator calls these practices demonic, and performance probably varied by status and occasion. Even so, mourning could be athletic, noisy, dangerous, and profoundly social rather than quietly private.

Israel ordered a major sacred tree cut down; priests and common people protested, while the ruler backed destruction and punished some ritual specialists. Conversion therefore involved coercion and conflict as well as preaching. The story's triumphant ending belongs to a missionary narrative and should not be mistaken for unanimous consent.

Golden interprets the 682 episode as conversion of Alp Ilutuer and his army within diplomacy, with no secure knowledge of Christianity's later fate among these Huns. Churches may have been built, but mass or durable conversion is unproven. Religious change could be official, local, mixed, temporary, or resisted.

Assemblies, feasts, races, wrestling, music, and skilled display made public life memorable. Their survival in a clerical account reflects what surprised or offended its author, not a complete cultural calendar. A source that notices sword fights at funerals may simply forget who swept up afterward.

sections.title: Learn, translate, speak, and bound the writing evidence

items.text: Education appears most clearly through missionary teaching: Israel preached with scripture, answered objections, trained or elevated priests, and was asked to remain as overseer and teacher. Interpreters and bilingual intermediaries were likely essential, but the narrative does not name a school, curriculum, enrollment system, classroom, or ordinary child's lessons.

Skills also passed through households, camps, military retinues, ritual specialists, and craft practice. Riding, herding, woodworking, diplomacy, song, and ceremony required learning even when no classroom appears. The sources reveal outcomes and elite spectacles, so apprenticeship is a cautious social inference rather than a documented Hunnic education law.

A Syriac tradition says the earlier missionary Kardost returned with books written in a Hunnic language. Scholars debate the people, date, translation, and script behind that notice. No surviving manuscript or inscription can be securely tied to the seventh-century Varachan polity, so it cannot supply a display sample.

The letters attributed to Alp Ilutuer survive inside an Armenian historical compilation, not as original Hunnic documents. The compilation itself has multiple authors and later transmission. Armenian wording can be quoted as evidence for the source tradition, but relabeling it “Hunnic script” would manufacture an artifact that does not exist.

Secure writing sample: none presently survives for this exact polity with a recoverable native text, script, object, and translation. The card explicitly records that absence. It excludes Attila-era names, later Old Turkic inscriptions, Caucasian Albanian palimpsests, and Armenian narrative prose because each belongs to a different community or transmission context.

sections.title: Face illness, injury, care, and uncertain medicine

items.text: The mission narrative mentions sickness, lesions, insanity, wounds, exhaustion, and death, mostly inside religious arguments. Ritual specialists claimed sacred powers could heal or punish; the bishop offered a rival explanation. These are beliefs reported by an opponent, not clinical case notes or proof that supernatural care was the only treatment available.

Cavalry, raids, wrestling, sword contests, travel, childbirth, animal work, and winter exposure created risks that households had to manage. The record does not name a Hunnic physician, midwife, surgeon, pharmacy, hospital, fee, or remedy. Practical care is likely, but its people and procedures remain undocumented.

Israel's party was delayed by severe snow, lost visibility, became exhausted, and rested for many days after reaching Varachan. The passage documents fatigue, shelter, pacing, and recovery during travel more securely than medicine. Prayer structures the author's explanation; supplies and hospitality still mattered to bodies on the road.

Horse and livestock health must have mattered to mobile households and cavalry, yet reviewed sources preserve no veterinary manual or named specialist from Varachan. Feeding, watering, sheltering, and treating animals should be presented as necessary work, not reconstructed technique. A valuable horse could not repair itself after a race.

Burial archaeology may eventually clarify trauma, diet, mobility, and disease, but the Chir-Yurt discussion used here emphasizes diverse graves and material culture rather than diagnoses. The card therefore avoids assigning life expectancy, epidemic causes, dental health, disability rates, or genetic ancestry to everyone called Huns.

sections.title: Find water and admit what sanitation evidence cannot show

items.text: The polygon spans Caspian lowlands, rivers, foothills, and mountain routes, but no source maps a Hunnic water network. People and animals necessarily used springs, streams, wells, carried water, or stored supplies according to place and season. Those are bounded necessities, not evidence for one standardized system.

Movses describes worship involving water and rain, drought relief, food growth, and a baptismal font. These references show water's ritual and ecological importance, not how homes fetched, stored, filtered, heated, or shared it. A sermon is unusually poor plumbing documentation, even when it mentions a font.

Derbent's inherited fortifications controlled a narrow coastal route and later phases included cisterns for garrisons. The dated cistern evidence does not demonstrate that seventh-century Varachan households used the same works. Regional infrastructure may frame possibilities, but neighboring monuments cannot be copied into the Hunnic capital.

No reviewed source securely documents toilets, latrines, sewers, drains, bathhouses, refuse pits, street cleaning, dung removal, wastewater rules, or municipal sanitation for the exact polity. Waste was handled somehow, especially around camps and animals, but the method, labor division, privacy, and public-health effects remain unknown.

Mobile camps could relocate some waste pressures, while a city and royal court concentrated people, animals, food, fuel, and discarded material. That contrast is an ecological inference, not excavated sanitation history. The card refuses both romantic cleanliness and automatic squalor; neither conclusion follows from silence in a missionary text.

sections.title: Measure achievements without turning legend into census

items.text: The polity's clearest achievement was maintaining a recognizable court, army, capital, diplomatic network, and regional identity between stronger neighbors. It could raid Albania, negotiate peace, host a mission, send ambassadors, and bargain through religious language. Power was real, although its territory and institutional reach cannot be measured precisely.

Varachan connected Caspian routes, foothill communities, mobile camps, and southern diplomacy. Reports calling it splendid or assigning tens of thousands of houses express importance but are not archaeological population counts. The achievement is a durable urban memory on a volatile frontier, not a confidently calculated metropolis.

The 682 encounter preserved unusually rich observations about crafts, ranks, envoys, ritual dispute, public performance, and political theology. That documentary survival is valuable, but it came through outsiders with missionary goals. Hunnic voices appear refracted through Armenian prose rather than as an archive written and preserved by local households.

Defending and traversing the Caucasian corridor demanded riding, provisioning, route knowledge, multilingual negotiation, and adaptation between camps and settlements. These collective capacities belonged to guides, herders, craftspeople, hosts, fighters, captives, and families as well as rulers. Elite titles alone did not keep horses fed or travelers warm.

The atlas polygon is useful for locating a broad story, but its perfect century and crisp seams exaggerate certainty. A historically responsible card can be an achievement too: it names the right Huns, preserves debate, counts every snapshot, and declines to promote colorful geometry into an eyewitness.

sections.title: End the polity in transformation and follow continuity

items.text: Arab forces under al-Jarrah campaigned north of Derbent in 723, striking settlements associated in later scholarship with the Hunnic-Savir zone. Warfare brought siege, capture, tribute, displacement, and provisioning demands. Because place-name equations differ, the card avoids presenting every reported Vabandar, Balanjar, Khamzin, and Varachan as automatically identical.

Marwan's vast 737 offensive broke through the Caucasus and forced a new political settlement with the Khazars. Later traditions connect it to the capture or destruction of Varachan. The card uses 737 as a circa endpoint because it marks a defensible transformation, not a perfectly witnessed dissolution decree.

Capture did not erase everyone living around Qaytaq, Sulak, Tarki, Semender, or the foothills. Communities, livestock practices, routes, kinship, languages, and religious mixtures continued under altered Khazar and Islamic-era arrangements. Political identity can vanish from chronicles while people remain, rename affiliations, move, intermarry, or serve new powers.

By world-800 the atlas assigns the tested core broadly to Khazars, but that visual replacement is not a safe automatic successor relationship. The Huns were already described as Khazar subjects, and regional power was layered. The override therefore records no predecessor or successor link rather than inventing a one-step transfer.

Keep exact id huns separate from hunnic-empire, sabirs, khazars, alans-700, and caucasian-albania. Their histories meet, and scholarly labels sometimes overlap, but the repository uses distinct records and geometries. The ending is transformation around 737: a polity loses separate visibility while residents and regional networks continue.

ending.text: Around 737, Marwan's campaign crossed the Caucasus during the decisive phase of the Arab-Khazar wars. Later Armenian and Arabic traditions connect the offensive with the capture or destruction of Varachan or related strongholds in the Country of the Huns. The evidence does not preserve a dissolution decree, a last securely named ruler, or a census of survivors, and disputed place-name equations prevent false precision. The event nevertheless provides a defensible endpoint for separate Hunnic political visibility at Varachan. Khazar power, Arab frontier administration, and local authorities reorganized the corridor; the atlas expresses this roughly by replacing the exact huns polygon with Khazar coverage at 800. Residents did not disappear with the label. Families, herders, cultivators, craftspeople, guides, ritual communities, captives, and soldiers continued, moved, intermarried, or adopted new affiliations. The card therefore marks transformation circa 737, records no automatic successor, and keeps the polity distinct from Attila's Hunnic Empire, neighboring Sabirs, and the Khazar realm in which it had already operated.
